source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC5330965 (Journal of Medical Toxicology 2017;13(1):71-87, online 20 December 2016; the published version as deposited, not an author manuscript), read in full in my own browser tab and saved to my scratch folder, including Tables 1 to 7, the search-strategy appendix, the Compliance with Ethical Standards section and the reference list. Figure 1 (bar chart of frequency of use) not viewed as an image; its counts are given in the Cumulative Synthesis text and Table 1. No online supplement.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim describes published cases descriptively, names the absence of comparison groups and of any denominator, and does not present resolution after stopping as proof of cause. It is more cautious than the review, whose Results call the listed features those with the highest sensitivity and whose Discussion speaks of moderate evidence that stopping is the definitive treatment.
claims.note: Every Sorensen number in the statement and magnitude re-found. Recomputed: the review truncates rather than rounds, so 154/211 = 73.0% (printed 72.9%), 157/170 = 92.4% (92.3%), 62/64 = 96.9% (96.8%), 192/197 = 97.5% (97.4%; at least weekly = 50 + 101 + 41 of the 197 with frequency specified), 151/197 = 76.6%, 134/179 = 74.9% (74.8%), 85/211 = 40.3% (40.2%); 45/179 = 25.1%, 65/179 = 36.3%, 30/179 = 16.8%, 39/179 = 21.8% as printed. The claim reproduces the printed values; harmless, but 154 of 211 is 73.0% if the editors prefer their own rounding. Points for the editor: (1) The median ages rest only on the 113 cases with raw data (n = 111, 84 and 101 equal the sums of the Table 1 rows without the 98-patient Simonetto series, which supplied only means), so they do not describe all 211. (2) The 62 of 64 is internally inconsistent in the source: the text attributes the two non-resolving patients to two case reports (Cox et al. 2012; Parikh & Gould 2010), while Table 1 puts one in the Soriano-Co series (4 of 5) and one among the case reports (37 of 38); Table 5 describes a Simonetto patient with no improvement despite self-reported abstinence while Table 1 counts that series as 6 of 6; and Table 1 heads the column 'relief with abstinence or reduction', so 'documented stopping' may include reduction. The claim states what the text says. (3) Return of symptoms on resuming use: Table 2 counts it as too inconsistently documented, as the claim says, but Table 5 relays that in Allen et al.'s series all 3 patients who resumed after a period of abstinence relapsed; the claim could add this. (4) Time to improvement with abstinence was listed for extraction (Data Collection) but never reported, which supports 'no time to resolution is reported'. (5) Frequency categories partly rest on recoding: 'heavy' use was coded as daily and 'frequent' as weekly (Data Analysis), and use was reported in incompatible units (Limitations). (6) On separating CHS from other cyclic vomiting, no study tested the proposed features' accuracy, as the claim says; the closest data are the second-hand cyclic vomiting surveys in Table 4, where hot showers were used by 72% of 31 and 67% of 437 patients with cyclic vomiting syndrome (81% of the latter used cannabis), which bears on how specific hot-bathing relief is.

anchors.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library searched from January 2000 to 24 September 2015, English only, plus a trial registry, dissertations, abstracts of four toxicology and emergency-medicine meetings and reference lists.

2,154 records plus 24 from bibliographies; 1,253 abstracts screened; 170 articles included (183 in the abstract). 88 case reports, 8 of them excluded (80 used), and 8 case series of four or more patients; no randomized trials of diagnosis, pathophysiology or treatment; quality too low for meta-analysis.

anchors.locator: Cumulative Synthesis, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Cumulative synthesis row and footnotes a and b)
anchors.extracted: 211 patients from the 80 case reports and 7 case series; the 98-patient Simonetto series entered as its authors' summary statistics (raw data unavailable) and the 31-patient Wallace series left out. 154 men (72.9%) and 57 women; median age at diagnosis 28 (IQR 22 to 34; n = 111), at first cannabis use 16 (14 to 18; n = 84), at symptom onset 24 (19 to 29; n = 101); use preceded symptoms in every case.

anchors.locator: Cumulative Synthesis, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Cumulative synthesis row)
anchors.extracted: Duration of use before symptom onset (179 patients): 1 year or less 45 (25.1%), 2 to 5 years 65 (36.3%), 6 to 10 years 30 (16.8%), 11 years or more 39 (21.8%). Frequency (211): more than daily 50 (23.7%), daily 101 (47.9%), weekly 41 (19.4%), less than weekly 5 (2.4%), not specified 14 (6.6%). Cyclic nausea and vomiting 100%; abdominal pain 85.1% (172 of 202); relief with hot baths or showers 92.3% (157 of 170).

Frequency of each characteristic among cases where it was reported: severe nausea and vomiting 100 (211); cyclic vomiting over months 100 (211); resolution after stopping 96.8 (64); hot baths with relief 92.3 (170); abdominal pain 85.1 (202); at least weekly use 97.4 (197); daily use 76.6 (197); regular use over 1 year 74.8 (179); male 72.9 and age under 50 100, both with the denominator printed as 227; all graded low. Return of symptoms on resuming use, normal bowel habits, negative workup and weight loss over 5 kg too inconsistently documented to count.

Of 64 patients with documented cessation, 62 (96.8%) had complete resolution of symptoms; the two without resolution had no urine testing to confirm abstinence (cited to two case reports); all 21 patients who did not abstain had ongoing symptoms. Stopping graded low here (very low in Table 5, moderate in the Discussion, 4th paragraph).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (Relief with abstinence or reduction column); Table 5 (Cessation of cannabis rows)
anchors.extracted: Table 1's resolution column covers abstinence or reduction and places the two non-resolvers in the Soriano-Co series (4 of 5) and among the case reports (37 of 38), not in two case reports; Table 5: Simonetto, of 10 followed up, 60% stopped and resolved, 30% continued with symptoms and one had no improvement despite self-reported abstinence (Table 1: 6 of 6); Allen, all 3 patients who resumed after abstinence had a return of illness; Wallace 30 of 31 (text and Table 1: 24 of 25).

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods › Data Collection, 2nd paragraph; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Time to improvement with abstinence was among the items to extract but no result is reported. Heavy use was coded as daily and frequent use as weekly; use was reported in variable units (cones, bongs, joints, grams per day). Frequencies reflect only what reports recorded, publication favours cases like the index description, and the criteria need validation in a prospective cohort.

Mean delay from symptom onset to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6; n not given). The authors say at least weekly use for over a year, severe cyclic vomiting with abdominal pain, resolution after stopping and hot-bathing relief have the highest sensitivity, a figure computed only among diagnosed cases.

Proposed characteristics, each graded low: severe cyclic vomiting usually with abdominal pain; onset preceded by at least weekly use; temporary relief with hot bathing; resolution with stopping; supportive features male sex, onset of use in the teenage years and symptom onset in the third decade. Of the cases with raw data, 85 (75.2%) met at least four and 104 (92%) at least three; the denominator is printed as 133, but the percentages correspond to 113 (211 minus the 98 summary cases).
Four case reports of patients first diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum and later with CHS; three cases caused by synthetic cannabinoids; follow-up documented for only 85 of 211 patients (40.2%).

Nine proposed mechanisms (CB1-mediated effects, slowed gut motility, plastic receptor changes, CB1 down-regulation with rebound, accumulation of metabolites, a non-THC plant compound, genetic variation in metabolising enzymes, partial agonism, splanchnic vasodilation), every one graded very low.

Second-hand surveys of cyclic vomiting syndrome: hot showers used by 72% of 31 patients (Namin) and 67% of 437 (Venkatesan, in which 81% used cannabis and bathing was associated with cannabis use, OR 2.54); no study tested how well the proposed features separate CHS from cyclic vomiting syndrome.
Prospective epidemiological studies are said to be needed to determine the prevalence of CHS and its rate of development among people who use cannabis; the review gives no such figure.

Recomputed: log-scale midpoint of 1.2 to 4.3 gives OR 2.27; implied two-sided P about 0.004 (at OR 2.54) to 0.012 (at the midpoint).

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low agreed: critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 13 not met (no protocol; English only from 2000; no list of excluded full texts and no flow diagram; no appraisal of included studies). Item 16 'yes' is lenient, since no statement covers funding for the review itself, but it is not critical and does not change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. All six gaps verified at the stated places (Cumulative Synthesis 4th paragraph; Discussion 4th, 5th and 9th paragraphs; Introduction 1st paragraph; Abstract).

missed: The two patients without resolution are attributed in the text to two case reports (references 8 and 56, Cox et al. 2012 and Parikh & Gould 2010, the latter a meeting abstract), while Table 1 places one in the Soriano-Co series (4 of 5) and one among the case reports (37 of 38); together with the Simonetto discrepancy in RI 4, the 62 of 64 is not reproducible from the source's own tables.
Table 1 heads the resolution column 'relief with abstinence or reduction', while the text calls the 64 'documented cannabis cessation'.

The median ages (n = 111, 84, 101) come only from the 113 cases with raw data: each n equals the sum of the Table 1 rows without the 98-patient Simonetto series, which reported only means (32.3 years at diagnosis, 25.3 at symptom onset).
Time to improvement of symptoms with abstinence is listed among the data extracted (Data Collection, 2nd paragraph) but no result is reported.
Return of symptoms on resuming use is counted as too inconsistently documented (Table 2), yet Table 5 relays that all 3 of Allen et al.'s patients who resumed after abstinence relapsed.
The printed percentages are truncated, not rounded: 92.3 (92.4), 96.8 (96.9), 97.4 (97.5), 74.8 (74.9), 40.2 (40.3), besides the 72.9 (73.0) noted in RI 2.
Minor: the Methods define the longest duration category as greater than 11 years, the Results and Table 1 as 11 years or more.
